front.title: The agent URI Scheme and Verifiable Agent Identity

abstract.t: Software agents increasingly act on the Internet on behalf of people and organizations: they call APIs, browse websites, and delegate work to other agents. Protocols such as A2A and MCP define how agents communicate, but there is no interoperable way to answer a prior question: which agent is this, and how can its claims be verified?

This document defines the agent URI scheme as a stable, human-readable identifier for an agent, a deterministic mapping from that identifier to an HTTPS-hosted Agent Identity Document, anchoring of the agent's keys to a web origin or a Decentralized Identifier, signed statements that bind the agent to its protocol metadata, and a profile of HTTP Message Signatures for automated traffic that lets an agent prove its identity on HTTP requests. It deliberately does not define how agents communicate, describe their capabilities, or are invoked.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: Agents are now first-class actors on the Internet. A single user task can cause an agent to call dozens of APIs and other agents, each of which needs to decide whether to serve the request. Today those services can see a TLS client, an IP address, perhaps an OAuth access token issued to some client, and a User-Agent string that anyone can forge. They cannot reliably tell which agent is calling, or whether the protocol metadata it advertises was really published by whoever controls it.

Communication protocols already exist. defines agent-to-agent interaction and an Agent Card; defines how agents reach tools and publishes server metadata; OpenAPI describes HTTP APIs. Each of these describes how to talk to an endpoint. None of them defines a portable answer to who an agent is that works across all of them.
This document defines that missing identity layer:

li.t: A name. The agent URI (e.g., agent://example.com/planner) is a stable, human-readable identifier for an agent ().
A document. Every agent URI maps to an HTTPS URL that serves an Agent Identity Document listing the agent's claimed operator, public keys, and links to its protocol metadata ().
An anchor. The agent's keys are trusted because of where the document is served, or because of a Decentralized Identifier bound to the agent URI ().
Statements. The agent signs statements binding itself to specific protocol metadata, so that metadata can be hosted anywhere ().
Proof on requests. The agent signs the HTTP requests it makes ().
Identify, do not invoke. An agent URI names an agent. It is not a locator for an endpoint and carries no invocation parameters.
One way to do each thing. There is one mapping from name to document, one key identifier, and one way for an agent to prove its identity on a request.
Reuse before invent. Every mechanism is a profile of an existing or in-progress standard: HTTPS and well-known URIs , JWK , JWS , HTTP Message Signatures as profiled by , and DIDs .
Anchor trust outside the document being verified. A key is trusted because of the origin or DID it is published under, never because a document names it about itself.
Authenticate keys, not claims. Verification establishes control of keys anchored to an agent URI. Everything else an agent says about itself, including who operates it, remains a claim.

section.name: Non-Goals
section.t: The following are out of scope:

li.t: Communication semantics, message formats, task lifecycles, and invocation. These belong to A2A, MCP, OpenAPI-described APIs, and similar protocols.
Capability, skill, or tool description. Protocol metadata documents (for example, an A2A Agent Card or an MCP server card) remain authoritative for these.
Credentials for short-lived agent instances, and bindings of agent keys to OAuth client authentication. These are expected to be specified in companion documents.
Verification of organizations. This document does not verify that the operator an agent claims is real or actually operates it.
Search, ranking, registries, reputation, pricing, and payments.
Authorization policy. Knowing who an agent is does not grant it anything.

section.name: Conventions and Terminology
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.
This document uses the terms "JSON object", "member", and "string" from , and "Dictionary", "Item", and "String" from .

dd.t: A software system that acts autonomously or semi-autonomously, typically on behalf of a person or organization.
The person or organization that an agent claims is accountable for it.
An agent URI as defined in . The human-readable name of an agent.
A JSON document, retrieved by dereferencing an agent URI, that lists the agent's claimed operator, keys, and links ().
The HTTPS URL that an agent URI maps to ().
The tuple ("https", host, 443) for the host of the agent URI.
A public key anchored to an agent ().
The JWK SHA-256 Thumbprint of an Agent Key ().
Any party that checks an agent's identity: a website or API receiving requests, an authorization server, a registry, or another agent.

section.name: Overview

figure.name: From agent URI to verifiable identity
figure.artwork: agent://example.com/planner (name) | | deterministic mapping v https://example.com/.well-known/agent/planner (AID URL) | +--------------------+---------------------+ | | | operator (claim) keys (JWK Set) links (rel, href) | | origin-anchored: trusted via HTTPS A2A Agent Card, DID-anchored: keys from DID document MCP server card, OpenAPI description

section.t: A typical verification, for a request received by an API:

li.t: The request carries an HTTP message signature and a Signature-Agent member whose value is the AID URL of agent://example.com/planner.
The verifier derives the agent URI from the AID URL and retrieves the AID (or uses a cached copy).
The verifier finds the anchored key identified by the signature and verifies the signature and the request content.

The verifier now knows that the request was made by a holder of a key anchored to agent://example.com/planner. It also has the operator the agent claims, which it must not treat as verified (). Whether to serve the request remains a policy decision.

section.name: Syntax
section.t: The following ABNF uses fragment from and ALPHA and DIGIT from .

figure.name: ABNF for the agent URI
figure.sourcecode:
agent-uri = "agent://" dns-name [ name-path ] [ "#" fragment ]
dns-name = label 1*( "." label ) label = let-dig [ *61( let-dig / "-" ) let-dig ] let-dig = ALPHA / DIGIT
name-path = 1*8( "/" name-segment ) name-segment = lc-let-dig [ *61( lc-let-dig / "-" ) lc-let-dig ] lc-let-dig = %x61-7A / DIGIT ; a-z, 0-9

section.t: Additional constraints:

li.t: dns-name MUST NOT exceed 253 octets, and its final label MUST contain at least one ALPHA character. Together with the ABNF, this excludes IPv4 addresses in dotted-decimal form and single-label names such as localhost.
Internationalized domain names MUST be represented as A-labels . IP literals, userinfo, ports, and queries are not permitted.
An agent URI with no name-path (e.g., agent://planner.example.com) identifies the domain's root agent.

section.t: Examples:

li.t: agent://example.com/planner#kPrK_qmxVWaYVA9wwBF6Iuo3vVzz7TxHCTwXBygrS4k (a reference to one of the agent's keys; see )

section.name: Normalization and Comparison
section.t: The canonical form of an agent URI is produced by:

li.t: Lowercasing the scheme and dns-name.
Converting any U-labels to A-labels.
Removing a ":443" port, or a ":" with an empty port, after the host.
Removing a single trailing "/" if present.

section.t: Parsers MAY accept input that differs from the ABNF only by the deviations corrected above, and MUST normalize it. Any other deviation (another port, uppercase in name-path, percent-encoding, dot-segments, a query, a trailing "." on the host) MUST be rejected.

Two agent URIs identify the same agent if and only if their canonical forms, with any fragment removed, are identical octet strings. In particular, agent://example.com/planner and agent://planner.example.com are different agents, even if the same operator runs both.
Agent URIs in AIDs, statements, and tokens MUST be in canonical form and MUST NOT contain a fragment, unless a fragment is explicitly permitted.

section.name: Dereferencing
section.t: An agent URI is dereferenced by mapping it to its AID URL:
For example:

table.name: Agent URI to AID URL mapping

section.t: The root agent uses the reserved segment _, which cannot appear in a name-segment. This allows the root AID and named AIDs to coexist on static file hosting, so an operator needs nothing more than the ability to serve static files over HTTPS for the domain.

The mapping is purely syntactic and reversible: an HTTPS URL is an AID URL if and only if it has no port, query, or fragment and applying the reverse mapping yields an agent URI that is valid and canonical. No registry or index needs to be fetched to dereference an agent URI.

section.name: Fragments
section.t: A fragment in an agent URI identifies an Agent Key by its Key Identifier (). No other fragment semantics are defined.

section.name: Format
section.t: An AID is a JSON object served with media type application/agent-id+json (). It has the following members:

dd.t: REQUIRED. String. The canonical agent URI that this document describes.
REQUIRED. Object stating who the agent claims is accountable for it, with members name (REQUIRED, string) and url (OPTIONAL, string, HTTPS URL). These values are self-asserted ().
REQUIRED for origin-anchored agents; MUST be absent for DID-anchored agents. A JWK Set containing the agent's public keys ().
OPTIONAL. String. A DID whose DID document is the anchor for this agent's keys ().
OPTIONAL. String. A display name for people. It has no identity semantics.
OPTIONAL. String. The time the document was last changed, as an RFC 3339 timestamp.

section.t: Members not defined here MUST be ignored by verifiers that do not understand them. Extension member names SHOULD be namespaced (e.g., "acme_tier") to avoid collision with future versions of this document.
An AID MUST NOT exceed 64 KiB.

section.name: Key Identifiers
section.t: Every Agent Key is identified by its Key Identifier: the base64url-encoded JWK SHA-256 Thumbprint of the key, computed as specified in for EC keys and in for OKP keys. This is the identifier uses for keyid. It is used everywhere a key is named in this document: JWK kid values in an AID, agent URI fragments, the JWS kid header of statements, and the keyid parameter of request signatures.

Verifiers MUST compute the thumbprint of each candidate key themselves and select keys by comparing it with the presented Key Identifier. They MUST NOT rely on an operator-supplied kid or DID verification method id to select a key. An AID or DID document in which two keys have the same Key Identifier MUST be rejected.
For DID-anchored agents, each verification method is converted to a JWK before the thumbprint is computed:

li.t: a publicKeyJwk value is used as-is (private members MUST NOT be present);
a publicKeyMultibase value that is a Multikey encoding of an Ed25519 public key (base58btc with the 0xed01 header, as defined in ) is converted to an OKP JWK with "crv": "Ed25519"; and
verification methods in any other representation MAY be supported; those a verifier cannot convert are ignored.

section.name: Key Purposes
section.t: For DID-anchored agents, a key is usable for assertion only if the DID document's assertionMethod relationship references it, and for authentication only if authentication references it .

For origin-anchored agents, a JWK MAY carry an agent_use member (): an array containing "assertion", "authentication", or both. A key without agent_use is usable for both purposes. A key whose agent_use is not an array of strings, or contains no recognized value, MUST be ignored.
Verifiers MUST enforce key purposes. Operators SHOULD give every key a single purpose, so that a key held by a running agent for signing requests cannot sign statements ().

section.name: Links
section.t: Each link object has the following members, with the semantics of Web Linking :

dd.t: REQUIRED. String. A registered link relation type or a URI.
REQUIRED. String. An absolute HTTPS URL.
OPTIONAL. String. The media type of the target.
OPTIONAL. String. An Agent Statement () about the target.

section.t: Link relations expected to be common include:

tr.td: An OpenAPI or other API description

section.t: For origin-anchored agents, a link whose href has the same origin as the AID Origin is trusted to the same degree as the AID itself. To compare, the verifier lowercases the href host, converts it to A-labels, and uses port 443 if none is present; the result must equal the AID Origin exactly (). No other normalization is applied. Every other link MUST carry a statement, and verifiers MUST ignore links without a valid one ().

For DID-anchored agents, every link MUST carry a statement signed with a key usable for assertion, and verifiers MUST ignore links without one; otherwise whoever controls the origin could replace linked metadata without holding any key authorized by the DID.

section.name: Retrieval and Validation
section.t: To obtain the AID for an agent URI, a verifier:

li.t: Parses and canonicalizes the agent URI (), rejecting it on failure.
Constructs the AID URL ().
Applies the fetch policy of .
Sends an HTTPS GET with Accept: application/agent-id+json, validating the server certificate for dns-name.

Treats any status code other than 200 (OK) , and other than 304 (Not Modified) received in response to a conditional request revalidating a cached copy , as a retrieval failure. Redirects are always failures.

Rejects responses larger than 64 KiB, or that are not valid JSON objects. Verifiers MUST NOT reject a response solely because its media type is application/json (to support static hosting) but MUST reject any other media type.
Rejects the document unless its id member is identical to the canonical agent URI.
Performs the anchoring checks of .

section.t: Verifiers SHOULD cache AIDs according to HTTP caching . Operators SHOULD NOT set a freshness lifetime longer than 24 hours, so that key removal takes effect promptly ().

section.name: Anchoring
section.t: An Agent Key is anchored when the verifier has established that whoever controls the agent URI published it. An AID uses exactly one of two anchoring modes.

section.name: Origin-Anchored Agents
section.t: The AID contains keys and no did. The keys are anchored by the HTTPS retrieval of : control of the AID Origin is control of the agent's identity.
Each JWK in keys MUST contain only public key parameters, have a kid equal to its Key Identifier (), have an alg member, and be usable for signatures ("use": "sig", or a key_ops containing "verify").
Implementations MUST support EdDSA (Ed25519) and ES256. Algorithms MUST be restricted as described in ; in particular, none and symmetric algorithms MUST NOT be accepted.
This mode needs nothing beyond static HTTPS hosting. Its weakness is that identity is exactly as durable as control of the domain ().

section.name: DID-Anchored Agents
section.t: The AID contains a did member and no keys. The agent's keys are the verification methods of the DID document, with the purposes defined in .

The binding between the agent URI and the DID MUST be bidirectional: the AID names the DID in did, and the DID document lists the canonical agent URI in its alsoKnownAs property . Verifiers MUST check both directions and MUST treat the agent as unverified if either is missing.

Pinning. A verifier that has previously verified an agent URI as DID-anchored and recorded its DID MUST NOT attribute a later AID for that agent URI to the same agent unless it names the same DID. An AID that is origin-anchored or names a different DID MUST be treated as a different identity (for example, by rejecting it, or by treating it as a new agent with no history), not as a key rotation.

Continuity and its limits. For a verifier that has pinned the DID, DID anchoring preserves identity across a rename or domain move: the operator publishes an AID under the new agent URI and adds that URI to alsoKnownAs. For a verifier with no prior state, DID anchoring gives no more assurance than origin anchoring ().

DID methods. A DID whose resolution depends on the same host as the agent URI (for example, did:web on that host) adds no independence from the origin. Operators SHOULD NOT use such a DID for DID anchoring, and verifiers MUST NOT treat it as providing assurance beyond origin anchoring. DID methods that support verifiable key-rotation history (for example, hosted independently of the agent URI's host) are RECOMMENDED. Verifiers MUST maintain an allowlist of DID methods they support and MUST reject any other method.

section.name: Lifecycle, Rotation, and Revocation
section.t: Removing a key from the AID (or DID document) revokes it: every statement it signed stops verifying once verifiers' cached copies expire. Rotation and revocation are therefore the same operation, and operators rotate as follows:

li.t: Publish the new key alongside the old one.
Re-issue all statements signed by the old key, including statements carried in AIDs copied by mirrors and registries.
Remove the old key once re-issued statements have propagated.

section.t: This document deliberately defines no list of retired keys: with a single way to stop trusting a key, verifiers never have to distinguish a planned retirement from a compromise. Statements about metadata that changes SHOULD carry an exp so that copies held by third parties are refreshed regularly.
If status is "suspended" or "retired", verifiers MUST treat all signatures and statements from the agent as invalid. A retired agent URI SHOULD NOT be reassigned to a different agent.

section.name: Agent Statements
section.t: An Agent Statement is a JWS in compact serialization, signed with an Agent Key usable for assertion, that binds the agent to a specific version of a resource such as an Agent Card. It allows protocol metadata to be served from any origin, mirrored, or included in registries without losing its link to the agent.
The JWS Protected Header MUST contain typ ("agent-statement+jwt"), alg (the algorithm of the signing key), and kid (the Key Identifier of the signing key). The payload is a JWT Claims Set with:

dd.t: REQUIRED. The canonical agent URI, without a fragment.
REQUIRED. The URL of the resource the statement is about.

REQUIRED. An object with members alg ("sha-256"), canon ("jcs" or "none"), and value (the base64url-encoded digest). With "jcs", the digest is computed over the resource canonicalized per ; with "none", over the exact bytes of the representation.

section.t: A statement protects only the bytes of the resource it names, not other resources that resource refers to.

section.name: Verification
section.t: To verify a statement carried in a link of an AID, a verifier:

li.t: Checks that typ is "agent-statement+jwt".
Checks that iss is identical to the AID's id, and checks the AID's status ().
Checks that sub is identical to the link's href.
Selects an anchored key usable for assertion whose Key Identifier equals kid, and verifies the signature.
Checks iat and, if present, exp.
Obtains the resource at sub, either by fetching it under the policy of or by using a copy, and compares its digest with resource_digest.

section.t: Statements obtained other than through an AID link (for example, from a registry) are verified in the same way, except that step 2 uses the AID retrieved for iss and step 3 compares sub with the URL the verifier intends to use.

section.name: Signing
section.t: An agent proves its identity on an HTTP request by signing it as specified in , with the additional requirements in this section. A request signed this way is a conforming request.
The request MUST include a Signature-Agent Dictionary member, keyed by the signature label, whose value is the agent's AID URL () and which carries the parameter type=agent-id:

figure.name: Signature-Agent member (line break for display only)

section.t: The signature MUST:

li.t: include created and expires, with expires no more than 300 seconds after created;
include a keyid equal to the Key Identifier of the signing key; and
include tag="web-bot-auth".

section.t: A nonce parameter SHOULD be included where the verifier is expected to detect replay.

figure.name: A signed request (line breaks for display only)
figure.sourcecode: POST /v1/bookings HTTP/1.1 Host: api.example.net Content-Type: application/json Content-Digest: sha-256=:...: Signature-Agent: sig1="https://example.com/.well-known/agent/planner" ;type=agent-id Signature-Input: sig1=("@method" "@authority" "@target-uri" "signature-agent";key="sig1" "content-digest"); created=1792486800;expires=1792486860; keyid="kPrK_qmxVWaYVA9wwBF6Iuo3vVzz7TxHCTwXBygrS4k"; tag="web-bot-auth" Signature: sig1=:...:

section.name: Verification
section.t: A verifier MUST perform all of the following steps, and MUST NOT rely on a generic HTTP Message Signatures implementation to enforce them:

li.t: Select the signature with tag="web-bot-auth" whose label has a Signature-Agent member with type=agent-id. If there is none, the request does not carry an agent identity under this document.
Check that the member value is exactly an AID URL, without normalizing it, and derive the agent URI from it by reverse mapping ().

Check that the covered components include every component required by , that expires is no more than 300 seconds after created, and that the current time is between them, allowing for modest clock skew.
Retrieve the AID () and check status ().
Select an anchored key usable for authentication whose Key Identifier equals keyid. Key lookup is keyed on the pair (agent URI, keyid), as required by .
Verify the signature as specified in .

If the request has content, recompute its digest as specified in and compare it with the covered Content-Digest value. A request with content and a missing, unsupported, or mismatched Content-Digest MUST be rejected, because a valid signature over Content-Digest does not by itself authenticate the content ().

section.t: On success, the verifier has established that the request, including its content, was made by a holder of a key anchored to the agent URI. On failure, the verifier MUST NOT treat the request as coming from the named agent; it MAY process it as an unauthenticated request.
A verifier that does not support type=agent-id ignores the member, as that specification requires, and so treats the request as not signed by a known agent rather than failing.

section.name: Use with OAuth
section.t: Identity is not authorization, and this document defines no new OAuth mechanisms. It adds one rule: only a request signature verified under establishes agent identity. OAuth client authentication, of any kind, authenticates an OAuth client, not an agent. An authorization server MUST NOT present a client to users, or record it, as a verified agent unless the request in question carries such a signature, and the agent it attributes is always the one derived from that signature.

Consent screens are reached through front-channel redirects that an agent cannot sign. An authorization server can therefore show a verified agent identity at consent only if the agent signed a back-channel request for the same authorization request beforehand. Agents that want this SHOULD use Pushed Authorization Requests and sign the pushed request. When a verified identity is shown, it MUST be the agent URI or DID, with the operator name presented as claimed by the agent ().

When an agent acts on behalf of a user or another agent, the delegation SHOULD be expressed with OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange , with the agent identified in the act claim by "sub" set to its canonical agent URI. As required by , only the current actor is relevant to access-control decisions.

Access tokens used by agents SHOULD be sender-constrained, for example with DPoP , using a key that is not an Agent Key usable for assertion. Resource servers MAY require a valid agent signature in addition to an access token.

section.name: Discovery
section.t: Dereferencing a known agent URI requires no discovery. To let others find which agents a domain operates, a domain MAY list them in an API catalog (a linkset ) at /.well-known/api-catalog, using the agent URI as the link context and agent-identity links to the AIDs:

figure.name: Listing agents in an API catalog

section.t: Publishing a catalog is optional (). Registries and search services that index agents SHOULD verify AIDs and statements themselves rather than asking clients to trust the index.

section.name: Trust Model
section.t: For origin-anchored agents, the trust anchors are DNS and the Web PKI: anyone who can obtain a certificate for the agent URI's host and serve content there can impersonate the agent. This is the same trust model as the web itself and is appropriate for most agents.

DID anchoring reduces this dependency only for verifiers that have pinned the agent's DID (). On first contact, a verifier cannot tell a legitimate origin-anchored agent from an attacker who has taken over the domain and replaced a DID-anchored AID with an origin-anchored one. Even for a pinned DID, assurance holds only if verifiers rely solely on DID-authorized keys and on metadata covered by statements made with them ().

section.name: Handle Reassignment
section.t: If a domain lapses and is registered by someone else, the new holder can publish an AID for the same agent URIs. Verifiers that record identities for audit or reputation SHOULD record the Key Identifiers (and DID, when present) alongside the agent URI, and SHOULD treat a change of all keys for an agent as a significant event.

section.name: Operator Claims
section.t: Verification establishes possession of a key anchored to an agent URI or DID. It does not establish who operates the agent: operator.name and operator.url are supplied by the same party that publishes the AID. The owner of attacker.example can claim "Example Travel Ltd" as operator and point operator.url at the real company's website.

User interfaces and logs MUST NOT present an operator name as verified unless it has been confirmed by a separate mechanism trusted by the verifier, which this document does not define. They SHOULD display the authenticated agent URI host (in A-label form) or DID alongside any operator name.

section.name: Verifier-Initiated Fetches
section.t: Verification causes network requests to destinations chosen by untrusted parties: AID URLs from Signature-Agent values, statement subjects, and requests made by DID resolvers. Each of these can be used for server-side request forgery or denial of service. The following policy applies to every fetch made in the course of verification:

li.t: Only HTTPS URLs are fetched, with certificate validation.

Destinations whose host is, or resolves to, an address that the IANA IPv4 or IPv6 Special-Purpose Address Registries mark as not globally reachable MUST NOT be fetched, nor hosts that are special-use names that do not resolve in the global DNS (for example, localhost or names under local or internal). Administrators MAY configure explicit exceptions for private deployments.
The resolved address MUST be checked and then used for the connection (pinned), so that DNS changes cannot redirect the request after the check.
HTTP redirects MUST NOT be followed, as in .
Verifiers MUST enforce timeouts and bound response sizes: 64 KiB for AIDs and a locally configured limit for other resources.

Verifiers MUST bound the number of fetches per verification; a limit of 4 (for example, the AID, a DID resolution, and a statement subject) is RECOMMENDED, with a DID resolution counting as one fetch and the requests a DID resolver makes bounded separately. Verifiers MUST NOT recursively follow links from fetched documents.
Verifiers MUST rate-limit fetches per host and cache results, including failures.

section.t: A statement whose signature is valid does not make its sub safe to fetch: an attacker can publish a legitimate AID under its own domain and sign a statement whose sub names an internal address.

section.name: Request Content and Replay
section.t: HTTP message signatures authenticate header values, not content. Verifiers MUST recompute Content-Digest over received content (); otherwise an attacker can change the content of a signed request while keeping the signed digest.

Signatures cover the method, target URI, and authority, which prevents replay against a different resource or service. The short created-expires window limits replay against the same resource; verifiers for non-idempotent operations SHOULD require and track nonce values.

section.name: Key Compromise
section.t: Compromise of an Agent Key lets the attacker act as the agent until the key is removed and caches expire. Operators SHOULD keep Agent Keys in hardware or a key management service, and SHOULD use separate keys for assertion and authentication (), so that compromise of a running agent does not let the attacker sign statements.

section.name: Cross-Origin Metadata
section.t: Requiring statements bound to the exact href for links outside the AID Origin (, ) prevents a compromised or malicious third-party host, mirror, or registry from attaching metadata to an agent's identity. A statement only proves that the agent published the resource; it does not vouch for the truth of the resource's contents.

section.name: Confusable Names
section.t: Agent URIs can be visually similar (e.g., agent://examp1e.example/planner and agent://example.example/planner). User interfaces that display agent identities SHOULD display the A-label form of the host, and SHOULD warn when an agent URI or DID is new to the user.

section.name: Privacy Considerations
section.t: The considerations of apply.

li.t: Linkability is the point, for agents. Request signatures make an agent's traffic attributable and linkable across services. That is intended for the agent; it must not extend to the people it acts for. Agent URIs and Signature-Agent values MUST NOT encode user identifiers.

Per-user agents. Deployments that create one agent per end user (e.g., agent://example.com/u/alice) make that user's activity linkable across all services the agent visits. Such deployments SHOULD use a shared agent identity and convey user context only through authorization tokens sent to parties entitled to it.

Enumeration. API catalogs () let anyone list a domain's agents. Domains that do not want their agents to be enumerable should not publish them in a catalog; AIDs remain retrievable by those who already know the agent URI.
Verifier fetches. Fetching an AID reveals to the operator that a verifier has seen the agent. Caching reduces this signal.

section.t: IANA is requested to register the following media types in the "Media Types" registry .

section.name: Signature-Agent Type
section.t: uses the Signature-Agent member parameter value type=agent-id. does not currently establish a registry of type values. This document asks that such a registry be created and that agent-id be registered in it, referencing of this document (see ).

front.title: Date and Time on the Internet: Timestamps

abstract.t: This document defines a date and time format for use in Internet protocols that is a profile of the ISO 8601 standard for representation of dates and times using the Gregorian calendar.

A Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) is a compact sequence of characters that identifies an abstract or physical resource. This specification defines the generic URI syntax and a process for resolving URI references that might be in relative form, along with guidelines and security considerations for the use of URIs on the Internet. The URI syntax defines a grammar that is a superset of all valid URIs, allowing an implementation to parse the common components of a URI reference without knowing the scheme-specific requirements of every possible identifier. This specification does not define a generative grammar for URIs; that task is performed by the individual specifications of each URI scheme. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

front.title: Augmented BNF for Syntax Specifications: ABNF

abstract.t: Internet technical specifications often need to define a formal syntax. Over the years, a modified version of Backus-Naur Form (BNF), called Augmented BNF (ABNF), has been popular among many Internet specifications. The current specification documents ABNF. It balances compactness and simplicity with reasonable representational power. The differences between standard BNF and ABNF involve naming rules, repetition, alternatives, order-independence, and value ranges. This specification also supplies additional rule definitions and encoding for a core lexical analyzer of the type common to several Internet specifications. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

front.title: Internationalized Domain Names for Applications (IDNA): Definitions and Document Framework

abstract.t: This document is one of a collection that, together, describe the protocol and usage context for a revision of Internationalized Domain Names for Applications (IDNA), superseding the earlier version. It describes the document collection and provides definitions and other material that are common to the set. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

front.title: Internationalized Domain Names in Applications (IDNA): Protocol

abstract.t: This document is the revised protocol definition for Internationalized Domain Names (IDNs). The rationale for changes, the relationship to the older specification, and important terminology are provided in other documents. This document specifies the protocol mechanism, called Internationalized Domain Names in Applications (IDNA), for registering and looking up IDNs in a way that does not require changes to the DNS itself. IDNA is only meant for processing domain names, not free text. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

front.title: Media Type Specifications and Registration Procedures

abstract.t: This document defines procedures for the specification and registration of media types for use in HTTP, MIME, and other Internet protocols. This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice.

This memo reiterates the assignment of an IPv4 address block (192.0.0.0/24) to IANA. It also instructs IANA to restructure its IPv4 and IPv6 Special-Purpose Address Registries. Upon restructuring, the aforementioned registries will record all special-purpose address blocks, maintaining a common set of information regarding each address block.

JSON Web Signature (JWS) represents content secured with digital signatures or Message Authentication Codes (MACs) using JSON-based data structures. Cryptographic algorithms and identifiers for use with this specification are described in the separate JSON Web Algorithms (JWA) specification and an IANA registry defined by that specification. Related encryption capabilities are described in the separate JSON Web Encryption (JWE) specification.

A JSON Web Key (JWK) is a JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) data structure that represents a cryptographic key. This specification also defines a JWK Set JSON data structure that represents a set of JWKs. Cryptographic algorithms and identifiers for use with this specification are described in the separate JSON Web Algorithms (JWA) specification and IANA registries established by that specification.

JSON Web Token (JWT) is a compact, URL-safe means of representing claims to be transferred between two parties. The claims in a JWT are encoded as a JSON object that is used as the payload of a JSON Web Signature (JWS) structure or as the plaintext of a JSON Web Encryption (JWE) structure, enabling the claims to be digitally signed or integrity protected with a Message Authentication Code (MAC) and/or encrypted.

front.title: Guidelines and Registration Procedures for URI Schemes

abstract.t: This document updates the guidelines and recommendations, as well as the IANA registration processes, for the definition of Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) schemes. It obsoletes RFC 4395.

This specification defines a method for computing a hash value over a JSON Web Key (JWK). It defines which fields in a JWK are used in the hash computation, the method of creating a canonical form for those fields, and how to convert the resulting Unicode string into a byte sequence to be hashed. The resulting hash value can be used for identifying or selecting the key represented by the JWK that is the subject of the thumbprint.

front.title: CFRG Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) and Signatures in JSON Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE)

abstract.t: This document defines how to use the Diffie-Hellman algorithms "X25519" and "X448" as well as the signature algorithms "Ed25519" and "Ed448" from the IRTF CFRG elliptic curves work in JSON Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE).

front.title: The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format

abstract.t: JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) is a lightweight, text-based, language-independent data interchange format. It was derived from the ECMAScript Programming Language Standard. JSON defines a small set of formatting rules for the portable representation of structured data.
This document removes inconsistencies with other specifications of JSON, repairs specification errors, and offers experience-based interoperability guidance.
This specification defines a model for the relationships between resources on the Web ("links") and the type of those relationships ("link relation types").
It also defines the serialisation of such links in HTTP headers with the Link header field.
This memo defines a path prefix for "well-known locations", "/.well-known/", in selected Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) schemes.
In doing so, it obsoletes RFC 5785 and updates the URI schemes defined in RFC 7230 to reserve that space. It also updates RFC 7595 to track URI schemes that support well-known URIs in their registry.

This specification defines a protocol for an HTTP- and JSON-based Security Token Service (STS) by defining how to request and obtain security tokens from OAuth 2.0 authorization servers, including security tokens employing impersonation and delegation.

front.title: JSON Web Token Best Current Practices

abstract.t: JSON Web Tokens, also known as JWTs, are URL-safe JSON-based security tokens that contain a set of claims that can be signed and/or encrypted. JWTs are being widely used and deployed as a simple security token format in numerous protocols and applications, both in the area of digital identity and in other application areas. This Best Current Practices document updates RFC 7519 to provide actionable guidance leading to secure implementation and deployment of JWTs.

Cryptographic operations like hashing and signing need the data to be expressed in an invariant format so that the operations are reliably repeatable. One way to address this is to create a canonical representation of the data. Canonicalization also permits data to be exchanged in its original form on the "wire" while cryptographic operations performed on the canonicalized counterpart of the data in the producer and consumer endpoints generate consistent results.

This document describes the JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS). This specification defines how to create a canonical representation of JSON data by building on the strict serialization methods for JSON primitives defined by ECMAScript, constraining JSON data to the Internet JSON (I-JSON) subset, and by using deterministic property sorting.

The Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) is a stateless application-level protocol for distributed, collaborative, hypertext information systems. This document describes the overall architecture of HTTP, establishes common terminology, and defines aspects of the protocol that are shared by all versions. In this definition are core protocol elements, extensibility mechanisms, and the "http" and "https" Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) schemes.
This document updates RFC 3864 and obsoletes RFCs 2818, 7231, 7232, 7233, 7235, 7538, 7615, 7694, and portions of 7230.

The Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) is a stateless application-level protocol for distributed, collaborative, hypertext information systems. This document defines HTTP caches and the associated header fields that control cache behavior or indicate cacheable response messages.
This document obsoletes RFC 7234.

This document describes a mechanism for creating, encoding, and verifying digital signatures or message authentication codes over components of an HTTP message. This mechanism supports use cases where the full HTTP message may not be known to the signer and where the message may be transformed (e.g., by intermediaries) before reaching the verifier. This document also describes a means for requesting that a signature be applied to a subsequent HTTP message in an ongoing HTTP exchange.

This document defines HTTP fields that support integrity digests. The Content-Digest field can be used for the integrity of HTTP message content. The Repr-Digest field can be used for the integrity of HTTP representations. Want-Content-Digest and Want-Repr-Digest can be used to indicate a sender's interest and preferences for receiving the respective Integrity fields.
This document obsoletes RFC 3230 and the Digest and Want-Digest HTTP fields.

This document describes a set of data types and associated algorithms that are intended to make it easier and safer to define and handle HTTP header and trailer fields, known as "Structured Fields", "Structured Headers", or "Structured Trailers". It is intended for use by specifications of new HTTP fields.
This document obsoletes RFC 8941.

front.title: HTTP Message Signatures for automated traffic

abstract.t:
This document describes a protocol for identifying automated traffic using [HTTP-MESSAGE-SIGNATURES]. The goal is to allow automated HTTP clients to cryptographically sign outbound requests, allowing HTTP servers to verify their identity with confidence.
It defines the Signature-Agent header field for in-band key discovery, a key directory format based on JWKS, and a well-known URI at which that directory is served.

front.title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels

abstract.t: In many standards track documents several words are used to signify the requirements in the specification. These words are often capitalized. This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words

abstract.t: RFC 2119 specifies common key words that may be used in protocol specifications. This document aims to reduce the ambiguity by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.

front.title: Additional Media Type Structured Syntax Suffixes

abstract.t: A content media type name sometimes includes partitioned meta- information distinguished by a structured syntax to permit noting an attribute of the media as a suffix to the name. This document defines several structured syntax suffixes for use with media type registrations. In particular, it defines and registers the "+json", "+ber", "+der", "+fastinfoset", "+wbxml" and "+zip" structured syntax suffixes, and provides a media type structured syntax suffix registration form for the "+xml" structured syntax suffix. This document is not an Internet Standards Track specification; it is published for informational purposes.

This document offers guidance for developing privacy considerations for inclusion in protocol specifications. It aims to make designers, implementers, and users of Internet protocols aware of privacy-related design choices. It suggests that whether any individual RFC warrants a specific privacy considerations section will depend on the document's content.

This specification defines the Security Event Token (SET) data structure. A SET describes statements of fact from the perspective of an issuer about a subject. These statements of fact represent an event that occurred directly to or about a security subject, for example, a statement about the issuance or revocation of a token on behalf of a subject. This specification is intended to enable representing security- and identity-related events. A SET is a JSON Web Token (JWT), which can be optionally signed and/or encrypted. SETs can be distributed via protocols such as HTTP.

This document defines the pushed authorization request (PAR) endpoint, which allows clients to push the payload of an OAuth 2.0 authorization request to the authorization server via a direct request and provides them with a request URI that is used as reference to the data in a subsequent call to the authorization endpoint.

front.title: Linkset: Media Types and a Link Relation Type for Link Sets

abstract.t: This specification defines two formats and associated media types for representing sets of links as standalone documents. One format is based on JSON, and the other is aligned with the format for representing links in the HTTP "Link" header field. This specification also introduces a link relation type to support the discovery of sets of links.

This document describes a mechanism for sender-constraining OAuth 2.0 tokens via a proof-of-possession mechanism on the application level. This mechanism allows for the detection of replay attacks with access and refresh tokens.

front.title: api-catalog: A Well-Known URI and Link Relation to Help Discovery of APIs

abstract.t: This document defines the "api-catalog" well-known URI and link relation. It is intended to facilitate automated discovery and usage of published Application Programming Interfaces (APIs). A request to the api-catalog resource will return a document providing information about, and links to, the Publisher's APIs.

section.name: Open Issues
section.t: This appendix will be removed before publication.

li.t: Signature-Agent type registry. has no registry for type values. Work with the webbotauth WG to create one, or to define agent-id there. Until then, verifiers that only implement ignore agent identities.

Back-references from protocol metadata. Agree with the A2A and MCP projects on how an Agent Card or MCP server card names its agent URI, and who registers the agent-card and mcp-server-card link relations.

Companion documents. Credentials for short-lived agent instances (in -04, a profile of the WIMSE Workload Identity Token) and bindings of agent keys to OAuth client authentication (in -04, private_key_jwt attribution) are to be specified separately, in coordination with the WIMSE and OAuth working groups.

Cryptographic test vectors. covers URI processing. Once an implementation can produce and cross-check them, add vectors for statement iss/sub binding, DID key conversion and per-purpose selection, agent_use enforcement, content tampering with a valid signature, fetches to forbidden destinations, and expired statements.

section.name: Changes from draft-narvaneni-agent-uri-04
section.t: This revision simplifies the document so that each task has one mechanism.
Removed or moved out:

li.t: Ports. Agent URIs no longer contain ports, so an agent's identity depends only on its host and name.
Instance credentials. The profile of the WIMSE Workload Identity Token moves to a companion document ().

OAuth client-authentication attribution. The association check, qualifying-key rules, and the agent_uri client metadata parameter are removed. Only a verified request signature establishes agent identity ().
The appendix listing changes from draft-narvaneni-agent-uri-03.

section.t: Added or completed:

li.t: Full IANA registration templates.
"One way to do each thing" as a design principle.

section.t: Closed open issues:

li.t: Retired keys: the re-issue model is kept, giving a single way to stop trusting a key ().

DNS-based verification: not adopted. Any operator that can obtain a TLS certificate for a domain can serve AIDs from static hosting, and a DNS alternative would need DNSSEC and a second verification path.
Reserved root segment and name-path rules: kept as specified.
Ports: removed.
